theory.overview: While combinational logic (gates) produces outputs based solely on current inputs, sequential logic remembers—the output depends on both current inputs and past history. Flip-flops are the fundamental memory elements of digital systems. These remarkable circuits can 'remember' a single bit indefinitely (as long as power is applied), forming the basis of all storage: registers, cache, RAM, and even the program counter that tracks which instruction to execute next. Understanding flip-flops unlocks the door to understanding how computers store and sequence information.

sections.title: The SR Latch: Memory Begins
sections.content: The simplest memory circuit uses cross-coupled NOR (or NAND) gates. Set (S) makes Q=1, Reset (R) makes Q=0. When neither is active, the circuit 'remembers' its previous state. The forbidden state (S=R=1 for NOR latch) must be avoided. This basic bistable circuit demonstrates the essence of memory: feedback creates stability.

sections.title: The D Flip-Flop: Controlled Storage
sections.content: The D (Data) flip-flop solves the SR latch's undefined state problem. It has one data input (D) and a clock input. On the clock edge (rising or falling, depending on design), the D value is captured and held at Q until the next clock edge. This synchronous behavior is essential for organized, predictable circuit operation. Most modern digital design uses D flip-flops exclusively.

timing.setupTime: Data must be stable before clock edge
timing.holdTime: Data must remain stable after clock edge
timing.clockToQ: Time from clock edge to stable output

sections.title: Clock Signals: The Heartbeat
sections.content: Digital systems use a clock signal—a periodic square wave that synchronizes all operations. Like a conductor's baton, the clock ensures all flip-flops update simultaneously, preventing chaos. Clock frequency determines performance: a 3 GHz CPU has a clock period of about 333 picoseconds. The maximum clock frequency is limited by the longest propagation delay through combinational logic between flip-flops.

sections.title: JK and T Flip-Flops: Specialized Behaviors
sections.content: The JK flip-flop eliminates the forbidden state of SR: when J=K=1, it toggles (flips) its output. This makes JK flip-flops ideal for counters. The T (Toggle) flip-flop is a simplified JK—when T=1, it toggles; when T=0, it holds. These specialized flip-flops are useful for frequency dividers and ripple counters.

sections.title: Registers: Multi-bit Storage
sections.content: A register is simply a group of flip-flops that store multiple bits together. A 32-bit register contains 32 D flip-flops sharing a common clock. Registers are the fastest memory in a computer, located directly within the CPU. They hold operands for arithmetic, memory addresses, and control information. Register transfer level (RTL) design describes how data moves between registers through combinational logic.

sections.title: Metastability: When Timing Fails
sections.content: If setup or hold times are violated, a flip-flop can enter metastability—a state where the output hovers between 0 and 1 for an unpredictable time. While the flip-flop will eventually settle, the delay can cause system failure. Designers use synchronizers (two flip-flops in series) when crossing clock domains to reduce metastability risk, though it can never be completely eliminated.
solutions: Allow extra clock cycles for settling

keyConcepts.name: Bistable Circuit
keyConcepts.description: A circuit with two stable states (0 or 1). Feedback creates memory.

keyConcepts.name: Setup Time (t_setup)
keyConcepts.description: Minimum time data must be stable before clock edge.

keyConcepts.name: Hold Time (t_hold)
keyConcepts.description: Minimum time data must remain stable after clock edge.

keyConcepts.name: Propagation Delay (t_clock_to_Q)
keyConcepts.description: Time from clock edge to valid output.

complexity.delay: Setup + Clock-to-Q determines minimum clock period

steps.title: Create Cross-Coupled Inverters
steps.description: Connect two inverters in a loop—output of one to input of other. This creates two stable states.

steps.title: Add Control Inputs
steps.description: Replace inverters with NOR or NAND gates to get Set and Reset inputs.

steps.title: Add Clock Synchronization
steps.description: Gate the inputs with a clock signal to create a D flip-flop that updates only on clock edges.

steps.title: Build Registers
steps.description: Array multiple flip-flops to store multi-bit values like bytes or words.

practiceProblems.title: SR Latch Behavior
practiceProblems.description: In an SR latch (NOR type), if S=1 and R=0, what is Q?
practiceProblems.explanation: S (Set) sets Q to 1. R is inactive (0), so no reset occurs.

practiceProblems.title: D Flip-Flop Timing
practiceProblems.description: When does a D flip-flop capture its input?
practiceProblems.explanation: D flip-flops are edge-triggered. The value at D is captured at the moment of the clock transition (rising or falling edge).

practiceProblems.title: JK Toggle Mode
practiceProblems.description: What happens when J=1 and K=1 in a JK flip-flop?
practiceProblems.explanation: J=K=1 is the toggle mode. Q becomes NOT(Q)—if it was 0, becomes 1; if 1, becomes 0.

practiceProblems.title: 8-bit Register Size
practiceProblems.description: How many D flip-flops are needed for an 8-bit register?
practiceProblems.explanation: Each flip-flop stores one bit. An 8-bit register needs 8 flip-flops sharing a common clock.

practiceProblems.title: Maximum Clock Frequency
practiceProblems.description: If setup time is 2ns, clock-to-Q is 3ns, and combinational logic delay is 10ns, what's the maximum clock frequency?
practiceProblems.explanation: Minimum period = setup + clock-to-Q + logic = 2 + 3 + 10 = 15ns. Frequency = 1/15ns = 66.7 MHz.

practiceProblems.title: Metastability Cause
practiceProblems.description: What causes a flip-flop to enter metastability?
practiceProblems.explanation: When data changes too close to the clock edge (setup/hold violation), the flip-flop may not resolve to a valid state quickly.

snippets.title: Flip-Flop Simulation
snippets.code:
class DFlipFlop:
    def __init__(self):
        self.q = 0
        self.q_not = 1
    
    def clock(self, d):
        # On clock edge, capture D
        self.q = d
        self.q_not = 1 - d
        return self.q, self.q_not

class Register:
    def __init__(self, width=8):
        self.bits = [DFlipFlop() for _ in range(width)]
    
    def load(self, values):
        result = []
        for i, bit in enumerate(self.bits):
            q, _ = bit.clock(values[i])
            result.append(q)
        return result
    
    def read(self):
        return [bit.q for bit in self.bits]

# Test 4-bit register
reg = Register(4)
print(f'Initial: {reg.read()}')  # [0, 0, 0, 0]

# Load 1010
reg.load([0, 1, 0, 1])  # LSB first
print(f'After load: {reg.read()}')  # [0, 1, 0, 1]

# Clock ticks but no change (load same values again)
reg.load([0, 1, 0, 1])
print(f'Stable: {reg.read()}')  # Still [0, 1, 0, 1]
